sections.text: Continuity — a colossal, four-and-a-half-metre-high granite sculpture shaped as an infinity loop, located in central Frankfurt, Germany. It was created by the Swiss architect and polymath Max Bill, who lived from 1908 to 1994, a prominent figure in modernism and concrete art.

Imagine a block of granite of some two hundred tonnes, freed from a quarry in Sardinia in the 1980s, carved into a work of art and shipped from Carrara around the coast of Europe through the Strait of Gibraltar, then carried up the Rhine and the Main, before finally being installed as a monumental infinity loop in the heart of the financial district of Frankfurt, Germany. At eighty tonnes, the finished sculpture has been called the largest granite monolith to be transported since the colossi of ancient Egypt. So what was the idea behind it, and what made it possible forty years ago?
In Continuity, I attempted to realize an idea that had long been present in my mind: the representation of an infinite space in infinite motion.

In Continuity, I intended to achieve something similar: a surface, a boundary. Purely theoretically, from a twin band — one that is twisted one and a half times around itself and fused with another that is twisted only half a turn — one could obtain a form similar to the endless loop, but with only one surface and one boundary. For reasons unknown to me, this did not come about. Thus Continuity, despite a theoretically different expected result, consists of two parallel, bounded surfaces, composed of infinitely many straight lines.

This explanation may seem somewhat dry and primitive, yet it is the only thing I can say about it myself. I can, however, add that for me such a sculpture represents something like a knot in space, a point of concentration of various latent directions, and that through its existence space is ordered, newly formed, and given aim and direction.

There is continuity in our purpose. However, our purpose is also to see — and to see clearly. We designers are not working for the sake of machines, for some impersonal, superordinate entity such as industry, or state, or community. We are working for the wellbeing of every person, every individual, as part of a community. This purpose, this new humanism, is what I'd like to see as continuity. — Max Bill, Continuity and Change, 1953.
Max Bill, who lived from 1908 to 1994, was a great Swiss polymath: architect, industrial and graphic designer, sculptor, painter — and also a prolific writer, scholar, and teacher.

He attended the Bauhaus, where he was taught by Josef Albers, László Moholy-Nagy, Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky and Oskar Schlemmer. Bill remained closely associated with the Bauhaus school and was a key figure in developing and propagating its principles — as a guest lecturer at the Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich, and as a co-founder and first rector of the Ulm School of Design.

As Deutsche Bank's Twin Towers rose in Frankfurt between 1979 and 1984, the board, on the initiative of Herbert Zapp, began in 1981 to search for a sculpture to stand at the threshold of the new headquarters. The criteria were clear: an artist from the German-speaking countries, a work of significant contemporary art that would address the plaza rather than the facade, and a free artistic solution that still reflected the functions of the bank.

The choice fell on Max Bill, whose art of precise geometry and mathematics, rooted in the Bauhaus, matched the bank's vision. Bill first proposed a coloured column, but when asked how he would decide in the board's place, he chose Kontinuität, the work also favoured by the bank's art advisers. Once destroyed by vandals in Zurich, the granite loop would now stand in contrast and harmony with the straight towers, an image of unbroken continuity in trade, banking and art itself.

At the sculpture's inauguration in 1986, Herbert Zapp — board member and initiator of the Deutsche Bank art collection programme, who had begun acquiring works to fill the bank's buildings seven years earlier — said:

Max Bill's sculpture does not simply correspond to the bank building. It occupies an urbanistically significant setting, and will be seen and rediscovered daily by many people. Whether from a car, a park bench, on foot, from the Opernplatz or from the Taunusanlage: from every angle, and for everyone who takes pleasure in it, this granite sculpture with its infinite loop is meant to be an offering, a point of reference.

In 1981, Max Bill met the young and energetic sculptor and photographer Dominique Stroobant. This encounter grew into a lifelong friendship. Their greatest challenge would become the project Continuity — the development of which took three years.

Stroobant was responsible for the entire production process: from planning the transportation route of a massive block of granite, to the creation of the full-scale, four-metre sculpture together with his team of four sculptors.

Dominique Stroobant is a Belgian artist and mathematician known for his work at the intersection of geometry, perception and conceptual art. His practice explores spatial structures, continuity, and transformation — often translating abstract mathematical principles into precise visual or sculptural expressions.
Finite infinity.

Bill first gave this idea a form in 1935 with the endless ribbon, a surface with one side and one edge. Its coincidence with the Möbius strip, which he learned of only later, was, he said, “an entirely fortuitous spark”. Kontinuität was meant to be another such surface: “one surface, one boundary”. It turned out otherwise. The sculpture has two surfaces with parallel boundaries, “for reasons unknown to me”.

Bill left the question open. We are certain that Kontinuität is a form of infinity. But which kind? And how can we find out? The method of verifiable logic points the way: what a work claims can be checked against the work. A granite monolith obviously cannot be unrolled to establish its topology. But the same form exists at a scale one can hold in the hands: the copper model Bill made in 1945–46, kept today at Haus Bill in Zumikon, Switzerland. It served as the topological prototype for every later Kontinuität, the plaster of 1947 and the granite of 1986 alike. We turned to it for our studies.

In Continuity, I intended to achieve something similar — a single surface, a single boundary. Theoretically, a double helix, twisted twice by half a turn and fused with one twisted only half a turn, should have resulted in something akin to an infinite loop, possessing only one surface and one boundary. For reasons unknown to me, this did not happen, so Continuity, despite the theoretically expected outcome, consists of two parallel bounded surfaces composed of infinitely many straight lines. This explanation may sound somewhat dry and simplistic, yet it is the only thing I can say about it myself. — Max Bill.

Our experiments were practical: we worked with a strip of paper. First we passed the strip along the band of the model to establish its length. Then the strip was folded step by step, applying the principle of origami and following the direction of every curve of the sculpture. This led us to an inspiring finding: Kontinuität is indeed a single band, turned four times through 180 degrees and closed on itself, a surface without beginning or end.

Granite of the quality the sculpture demanded is quarried in only a few places in the world, among them Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Sardinia. Sardinia was chosen for its accessibility: the quarry lay so close to the sea that the monolith could reach the ship without crossing a single bridge, and travel on to the workshops of Carrara.

The search for the stone began before there was anyone to cut it. On 25 April 1983 the “Esagono” work collective was formed — the group of sculptors and technicians who would spend the next three years on a single object. Five months later, on 13 September, Max Bill travelled to Sardinia with Rodolfo Costantino to inspect the Scarraciana quarry in the island’s north-east, looking for a block large enough, and sound enough, to survive what was about to be done to it.

They found it there. On 20 October 1983 the charges were set and a block of some 500 tons was blasted clear of the rock face — many times the weight of the finished sculpture, because the finished sculpture had to come out of a single uninterrupted mass. Nothing about Continuity could be assembled from parts. Every curve had to already be present inside the stone, waiting to be found.
